newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German manufacturing growth gains pace - PMI.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German manufacturing growth gains pace - PMI.

text.p: Germany's manufacturing sector expanded at an accelerated pace in May as more bottlenecks emerged, driving up prices, according to the BME/Reuters German Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI).
The index, first published last month, rose to a seasonally-adjusted 57.49 in May, the highest level yet recorded after 56.58 in April, research group NTC Publications Ltd said on Monday.

The data, showing the ninth consecutive monthly rise, also revealed a new trend of rising domestic demand which complemented the export growth that has been the main driving force behind Germany's sluggish upturn over the past year.
NTC also said that for the first time since its survey began in April 1996, companies did not report an overall decline in employment.

"Output, orders, purchasing and employment indexes all reached new highs," NTC said. The new orders index within the PMI rose for the eleventh consecutive month and reached a record 60.96, up from 60.39.
Suppliers were running short of production capacity to meet rising demand.
That, coupled with the higher cost of imported materials from the continued weakness of the mark, caused prices paid for supplies to rise for the fourth month in a row, NTC said.

The PMI, modelled on the closely watched U.S. National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index, is designed to provide an overall view of activity in the manufacturing sector and acts as a leading indicator.
Analysts said the data confirmed German economic growth was picking up at a moderate pace but that wage pressures were still too weak to stoke up inflation.
Meanwhile, the labour market remained in the doldrums even though employers were reporting a halt to the drop in employment, analysts said.

"The uptrend is still intact and the figures do not show the economy is really picking up tremendously in speed. The employment situation is still dire," said Timo Klein, an economist at research group MMS International.
The PMI is based on a survey of 350 companies carried out by NTC in cooperation with the BME German Association for Materials Management, Purchasing and Logistics.

A reading below 50 percent indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally declining, while a level above 50 percent shows it generally expanding. The more it deviates from 50, the greater the improvement or decline in the current month.
The price index component of the PMI rose to a seasonally-adjusted 55.98 in May from 55.04 in April. The employment index rose to 50.00 from 47.85.
